narrative.title: Why this territory, why now
narrative.body:
I spent the first part of my career in institutional finance, most recently at Goldman Sachs, managing 20+ client relationships across multi-million dollar accounts. The real skill there wasn't the numbers. It was earning the trust of busy, guarded decision makers, reading what each one actually needed, and staying fluent enough in dense material to solve real problems with them. In 2023, I stepped back to raise my two kids.

In 2025, I watched a stranger save someone's life during a medical emergency, and it pushed me to earn my EMT license. I finished in the top 5% of my cohort at UT Dallas. During clinicals I worked in the emergency department, on patient transfers, and in the ambulance, and completed coursework in pharmacology fundamentals. What stayed with me was how often a patient's outcome traced back to whether the right treatment reached them, and whether the provider treating them had the right information at the right moment. That is the part of the chain a territory manager owns.

I know what my resume does not have: a title that reads B2B outside sales. What it does have is the underlying work that requirement is meant to prove. As a full time volunteer representative across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, I ran a three state territory for 18 months with my own CRM pipeline, a written plan before every visit, a follow up review after every one, and hard weekly targets. I grew that territory almost entirely through referrals, not a warm list, by earning the trust of local advocates who opened doors a cold visit never would. That is territory planning, gatekeeper access, and rejection tolerance, learned the hard way instead of in a training program, and it sits alongside the account ownership I practiced every day managing 20+ relationships at Goldman Sachs.

I also bring two things a lot of candidates coming out of a traditional B2B seat don't. I am clinically fluent, so I can hold a real conversation with an endocrinologist, an OBGYN, or a primary care office on day one instead of spending months learning the vocabulary, and that same clinical grounding is where my comfort with prior authorization and pharmacy pull through starts. And I'm bilingual in Spanish, which across DFW physician offices means genuine rapport with the front office staff who decide whether you get five minutes or none.

I live in the DFW metro, my kids are in preschool with full time childcare in place, and I'm looking for a territory where I can put that grit to work for a company that, like Alora, is willing to go where it's needed.

startStories.title: Building a Territory Business Plan
startStories.teaser: Deciding who to call on, how often, and why, then hitting the number.
startStories.body:
At Vivint, I wasn't in the field, I was setting the targets the field reps had to hit. I diagnosed the performance gaps and built the forecasting models that became a $2M+ business case for senior leadership. That is the planning side of a territory number: understanding where it should come from before anyone chases it.

At Goldman Sachs, hitting the number meant something more literal: 10 to 20 complex transactions a week with zero defect accuracy, in a 70+ hour work week with no room for error. That is the same discipline it takes to consistently hit a quota month after month across a physician panel.

startStories.title: Pre-Call Planning & Follow Through
startStories.teaser: How I built a call planning habit from scratch in a three state territory.
startStories.body:
As a volunteer representative across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, I built this process myself. Before every visit I wrote a specific objective. After every visit I ran a follow up review, tracked through a CRM pipeline, capturing the concerns I heard so I could handle them better next time. That habit turned an underperforming territory into one of the strongest in the region.

At Goldman Sachs, the same instinct showed up differently. When a senior client pushed back on a contract term, I found the issue myself, got internal leadership aligned, and closed it out before it became a lost account. Prepare for the objection, then close with a clear next step, works the same whether the stakes are a contract or a prescribing decision.

startStories.title: Trusted Relationships With Gatekeepers
startStories.teaser: What I learned from the one gatekeeper everyone said not to bother with.
startStories.body:
The clearest example is a community leader I worked with as a volunteer representative, the gatekeeper to an entire network of prospects. He hadn't worked with anyone from our group in years, and everyone before me said not to bother. Instead of pushing him directly, I built a relationship with his wife over weekly lunches until I learned he missed playing soccer with a group he'd lost touch with. I organized a recurring soccer event and told him all he had to do was show up. He did, and over time he went from ignoring us completely to mobilizing his own network on our behalf. Resistance is usually just information about what someone actually values, which is as true for a front office gatekeeper as it is for a mission contact.

At Goldman Sachs, I managed 20+ relationships with decision makers who had every option available to them and no obligation to stay. Relationship first account management, reading what each one needed and delivering it, is what kept them.

startStories.title: Clinical Fluency in the Room
startStories.teaser: What EMT training taught me about talking with physicians and their staff.
startStories.body:
My EMT training put me in the emergency department, on patient transfers, and in the ambulance, working daily alongside physicians, nurses, and trauma teams under real pressure, plus coursework in pharmacology fundamentals. Assisting an ER physician during a high acuity emergency procedure, and supporting patients through the trauma bay while following compliance and documentation standards, taught me to stay calm and execute under pressure while working across a full care team.

That is the same comfort a territory manager needs walking into an endocrinologist's or OBGYN's office: enough clinical grounding to have a real conversation on day one, and enough respect for the process to understand where a prior authorization or a pull through step fits into a patient actually getting their medication.

startStories.title: Developing Advocates & Referral Networks
startStories.teaser: Finding the person whose voice already carries weight, and earning it on their terms.
startStories.body:
During my 18 months as a volunteer representative, each area had a community leader who was essentially the gateway between local members and our work. Without his engagement we were cut off from the exact network our prospects needed. Mine hadn't worked with anyone from our group in years, and everyone before me said not to bother.

So instead of pushing him directly, I built a relationship with his wife first, weekly lunches, genuine friendship, listening for anything that told me who he actually was. She eventually mentioned he missed playing soccer, so I organized a community soccer event and told him all he had to do was show up. He came, we made it recurring, and over time he went from ignoring us completely to making referrals and mobilizing his entire network. That is the motion this work takes: find the person whose voice already carries weight, develop them on their own terms, and let their credibility open doors a cold visit never could.

startStories.title: Reading a Territory With Data
startStories.teaser: Using data to find where the effort should actually go.
startStories.body:
At Vivint, I diagnosed territory level performance gaps and built executive forecasting models in SQL, Snowflake, and Python to understand exactly where the market was moving and why.

At 1-800 Contacts, I built a nationwide marketing heat map across 42,000+ U.S. ZIP codes to identify underperforming spend and high potential growth areas, then personally trained the Analytics team on how to use it. That is the same coverage and frequency thinking a territory business plan requires, and the same habit of sharing what I find rather than sitting on it.
